title: Motion: taking steps
subtitle: limp, stagger, trudge, flow, take a decisive step
summary: Learn precise verbs of walking and movement, the metaphors English builds on them, the water verbs used for crowds of people, and the adjectives that collocate with taking steps.

lesson.heading: Verbs of walking
rows: drunk, ill, or on a moving ship
lesson.note: The choice of verb tells the reader far more than walk ever could: an unsteady walker staggers, a weary one trudges, a proud one struts.

lesson.heading: More walking verbs
lesson.text: A few more movement verbs are worth adding to the set. Each one carries its own reason for moving that way, and that reason is what you really have to learn.

examples.note: file = move in a straight line, one after the other, so that large numbers can be controlled
saunter = walk in a relaxed, confident way, for pleasure

examples.text: He **sidled** up to me with a strange smile.
examples.note: sidle = approach someone in a slightly sneaky way, intending something dishonest or unpleasant

examples.text: Graceful dancers seem to **glide** across the stage.
examples.note: glide = move smoothly, as if not moving your feet at all

examples.text: Guests were **milling around** with glasses in their hands.
examples.note: mill around = lots of people moving in different directions, meeting and talking

lesson.heading: Movement verbs used metaphorically
lesson.text: English constantly borrows these verbs for situations where nobody is walking at all. The physical picture survives, so a project that **limps** is going badly and a government that **lurches** looks out of control.

examples.text: The maths lesson **limped** to a conclusion and everyone thankfully left the room.
examples.note: It was neither successful nor enjoyable.

examples.text: Let's **hop off** the bus at the next stop.
Miguel's business **staggered on** for a few years and then finally collapsed.
examples.note: It was clearly in difficulties long before it failed.

examples.text: Lisa did **staggeringly** well in her exams.
examples.note: staggeringly = amazingly; nobody expected her to do that well

examples.text: The government has **lurched** from one economic crisis to the next.
examples.note: It gives the impression of being out of control.

lesson.heading: More metaphors of motion
lesson.text: Three more are especially common. Notice that **trample on** takes an object you can damage - dreams, rights, feelings - and that **chase** someone can simply mean sending reminders about money they owe.

examples.text: Maria takes everything that life throws at her **in her stride**.
examples.note: take something in your stride = deal with it calmly, without being upset. She is an easy-going, relaxed person.

examples.text: Parents and teachers should try not to **trample on** children's dreams.
examples.note: trample on = destroy or spoil, for example by laughing at them

examples.text: If the Campbells don't pay their bill this week, you'll have to **chase** them.
examples.note: chase someone = phone, email or write to remind them

examples.text: After several **stumbling** attempts at writing, Theo finally had a poem published.
examples.note: stumbling = hesitant and uneven in quality, not at all confident

lesson.heading: People move like water
rows: Crowds of tourists **flowed** across the square all day long.
As soon as the school doors opened, children **spilled** out into the playground.
falling out in an uncontrolled way, suddenly, in all directions
People **streamed** into the lecture hall and soon there was standing room only.
a lot of people moving at a fairly constant pace from one direction
People have been **pouring** into the exhibition all day.
coming all the time, in large numbers, possibly from all directions
A **trickle** of people appeared outside and by midday a crowd had gathered.
only a few people, here and there
We **meandered** round the town, window shopping to our hearts' content.
not going in a straight line, with no definite purpose
Refugees have been **flooding** across the border since the start of the war.
coming in large numbers, spreading in all directions

lesson.heading: Taking steps
lesson.text: When you walk you take **steps**, and in metaphor you take steps too - towards a goal, or away from one. These adjectives are the ones that regularly go with **take a step** or **take steps**.

examples.text: Closing the library would be a **backward step**.
Signing the treaty was a **decisive step** towards peace.
It is a **giant step** for the company and an **unprecedented** one for the industry.
The government must take **urgent first steps** to cut emissions.

lesson.note: Other common choices: a big step, a critical step, a major step, a significant step.

lesson.text: In metaphor people take backward, decisive, major steps - never ~~footsteps~~. Footsteps stay literal, or appear in *follow in someone's footsteps*.

exercises.prompt: Match each walking verb with the reason someone moves that way.
Who would probably do each of these things?

pairs.left: someone anxious to make you like them
tourists exploring a city in a relaxed way

exercises.prompt: The old man ___ wearily homeward, his shoulders hunched in the rain.
exercises.explanation: If you strut you hold your chest out proudly, so you cannot have hunched shoulders or be weary. Trudge = walk heavily and slowly because you are tired.

exercises.prompt: The mother ___ across the bedroom, doing her best not to wake the baby.
exercises.explanation: Heavy trudging steps would wake a light sleeper. Tiptoe = walk quietly on your toes so as not to be heard.

exercises.prompt: Look at all those baby rabbits ___ across the field!
exercises.explanation: Stamping is far too heavy for a small animal. Rabbits, like birds, hop.

exercises.prompt: Ever since he had an accident last year, he has ___ a bit.
exercises.explanation: Stamping goes with anger, not with injury. After an accident a leg hurts, so you limp.

exercises.prompt: The drunken men ___ unsteadily out of the pub at closing time.
exercises.explanation: Striding is purposeful and cannot be unsteady. Staggered (or lurched) is the verb for unsteady, drunken movement.

exercises.prompt: Please try not to ___ on the daisies - they look so pretty in the grass.
exercises.explanation: Daisies are far too small to be stumbled on. Trample on = press down repeatedly with your feet and destroy.

exercises.prompt: The small dog ___ after the postman and caught his trouser leg in his teeth.
exercises.explanation: Tramping is slow and heavy, so the dog would never have caught him. Chase = move quickly after someone in order to catch them.

exercises.prompt: The new traffic system allows vehicles to ___ across the city without major disruptions.
exercises.explanation: Flow = move smoothly and without stopping.

exercises.prompt: There were such a lot of people at the talk that some were ___ out into the corridor.
exercises.explanation: Spill out = come out in an uncontrolled way because there is no more room.

exercises.prompt: When I have a day off, I like to ___ around town without a care in the world.
exercises.explanation: Meander = wander about with no straight route and no definite purpose.

exercises.prompt: We expected to be very busy during the sale, but there was just a ___ of people throughout the day.
exercises.explanation: A trickle of people = only a few, arriving here and there.

exercises.statement: If a lesson *limped to a conclusion*, it was lively and enjoyable.
exercises.explanation: The opposite. A lesson that limps to a conclusion is slow, weak and not at all enjoyable.

exercises.statement: Someone who takes everything *in her stride* deals with problems calmly.
exercises.explanation: Take something in your stride = handle it without being upset by it.

exercises.answer: Closing the library would be a backward step.
exercises.explanation: In metaphor you take a backward step, never a backward footstep.
